1. Introduction
Over the past two years, many visual foundation models
have emerged [4, 21, 23, 25, 27, 31, 44, 58, 63], achiev-
ing high accuracy on tasks like depth prediction, segmen-
tation, human parsing, normal estimation, few-view recon-
struction, and motion tracking. These models leverage su-
pervised learning on large, diverse datasets, achieving im-
pressive accuracy and remarkable generalization. However,
these advances have not translated to 4D (time + geometry)
modeling, a longstanding challenge in computer vision. We
see two main reasons: first, collecting high-quality, ground-
truth 4D data from real-world environments remains com-
plex and resource-intensive. Second, 4D understanding is a
holistic problem involving interconnected tasks like camera
pose estimation, 3D reconstruction, and dynamics tracking.
Although each subtask shows progress, data-driven cues re-
main noisy, and more importantly, unifying them synergisti-
cally for holistic modeling remains challenging. This paper
seeks to answer: Can we harness the success of visual foun-
dation models for dynamic 4D modeling?
In this paper, we propose Uni4D, a novel framework
that reconstructs 4D scenes from a single video captured
in the wild. Our method integrates data-driven foundation
models and conventional model-driven dynamic structure-
from-motion, combining data-driven cues and model-based
knowledge synergistically. Our intuition is simple: each
data-driven visual cue, such as video segmentation, pixel-
level motion tracking, and video depth, is a partial pro-
jection from the 4D world to the 2D video.
The key is
to create a 4D scene representation that coherently aligns
with each cue while incorporating strong prior knowledge

divide-and-conquer pipeline that progressively incorporates
camera poses, static geometry, and dynamic geometry and
motion into the optimization framework. Uni4D leverages
pretrained foundation models across different tasks, requir-

We demonstrate the effectiveness of Uni4D on various

2. Related Works
Structure from Motion and SLAM.
Structure from Mo-
tion (SfM) is a classical problem in computer vision that
aims to jointly recover camera parameters and 3D structure
from images [2, 10, 41, 47, 48]. Simultaneous localization

era parameters and 3D points, also known as bundle adjust-
ment [55]. This relies on the key assumption that the scene
being viewed is rigid (“static”), making these approaches
not applicable to dynamic scenes.

The problem of non-rigid structure
from motion is highly ill-posed. Previous works on non-

and vehicles [18, 37]. The generality of such methods is
limited by their category-specific nature. Recently, several
works have also begun to leverage trained neural networks
as priors for 4D understanding in a more freeform man-

the strategy further and integrates pretrained models in a
completely modular manner, fully unleashing their gener-

studied 4D reconstruction in an optimization-based frame-

3.3. Optimization Pipeline
We propose a three-stage optimization pipeline that
progressively incorporates camera pose, static geometry, and
dynamic geometry into the optimization framework. The
 stages are designed to tackle the most challenging and re-
 qwesting parts of the problem first, while maintaining the
 benefit of a global optimization framework.

Stage 1: Static Bundle Adjustment.
We start by fixing camera parameters and 3D static geometry, and optimize the camera poses and static geometry to fit the observed pixel tracks. This is a standard problem in SfM, but we have strong priors on the static geometry from the segmentation cues and initial depth estimation. The optimization is performed using bundle adjustment, which is known to be effective in monocular SfM for static scenes [2, 10, 41, 47, 48]. 

Stage 2: Dynamic Structure and Motion.
Once the camera poses and static geometry have been
 optimized, we move to the dynamic part. We use the segmentation
 cues and motion tracklets to initialize the dynamic 3D
 structure and camera motion. We then perform non-rigid
 bundle adjustment, which optimizes the dynamic 3D structure
 and motion to fit the observed pixel tracks. This stage uses
 the initial estimates from the previous stage and applies
 non-rigid bundle adjustment to refine the dynamic geometry
 and motion. 

Stage 3: Full 4D Geometry Fusion.
Finally, we combine the results from the first two stages
 to perform a final fusion of the static and dynamic geometry.
 We use the initial estimates from the previous stage and apply
 a non-rigid bundle adjustment that optimizes both the static
 and dynamic parts simultaneously, using the segmentation
 cues and initial depth estimates to enforce consistent
 geometry across space and time. 

This three-stage optimization pipeline is designed to pro-
gressively incorporate the most challenging parts of the
problem first, while maintaining the benefit of a global
 optimization framework.

4. Related Works
We discuss various approaches to 4D understanding
 and structure from motion. The traditional SfM and SLAM
 approaches focus on static scenes. Recent works have tried
 to extend these methods to dynamic scenes, but the lack of
 strong priors on geometry and motion makes it difficult to
 recover accurate 4D geometry. 

We also review the 4D understanding methods that lever-
age neural networks as priors. Some recent works have
started to use neural networks to learn representations of
4D objects, but these methods involve either training new
 networks or optimizing specific layers of existing networks.
 Our method takes a completely modular approach, fully
 leveraging pretrained visual models without task-specific
 retraining.

We compare our approach to other 4D reconstruction
 methods, such as Casu-SAM [68], MonST3R [65], and
 others, and demonstrate superior performance in both
 camera pose and geometry accuracy on the Sintel dataset.
 
5. Method
5.1. Pretrained Visual Cues
We first extract foundation models to obtain visual cues,
including dynamic segmentation, video depth, and motion
tracking. We use a collection of the most recent and effec-
tive models for these tasks, such as RAM for segmentation,
Co-TrackerV3 for dense motion tracking, and UniDepthv2
for depth estimation. 

5.2. Energy Formulation
We then formulate an energy minimization problem to
solve for 4D scene reconstruction. The energy is composed
of several terms that enforce consistency between the input
 cues and the 4D geometry. 

5.3. Optimization Pipeline
We employ a three-stage optimization pipeline that starts
with bundle adjustment for static geometry, then non-rigid
 bundle adjustment for dynamic structure, and finally a
 fusion step that combines both static and dynamic components
 to obtain the final 4D reconstruction.

6.1. Datasets
We evaluate our method on two datasets: DAVIS
 and Bonn. These datasets provide rich 2D and 3D data for
 evaluating 4D reconstruction methods. 

6.2. Metrics
We use metrics such as 3D ATE for camera pose, and
4D ATE for overall 4D reconstruction. 

6.3. Qualitative Results
We showcase qualitative results on several videos, demon-
strating the ability of our method to reconstruct both static
and dynamic 3D geometry accurately.

Dense Motion Tracking.
We use dense pixel tracking to
establish correspondences over time, which serve as mo-
tion cues to assist inference of geometry reconstruction and
dynamic object 3D motion. Unlike traditional 4D recon-
struction methods relying on optical flow [65, 68], dense
motion tracklets yield more correspondence pairs across
large viewpoints and structural changes. Pixel tracking also
outperforms sparse matching in density and surpasses flow
propagation in robustness, making it ideal for dynamic 4D
reconstruction.We utilize Co-TrackerV3 [22] for its robust-
ness, as it employs a 4D cost volume with an attention
mechanism to track 2D points through occlusions, recently
proving to be effective for dynamic neural rendering. We
apply Co-Tracker bi-directionally on a dense grid every 10
frames to ensure thorough coverage. We filter and classify
tracklets using segmentation masks yielding a set of cor-
respondent point trajectories {Zk ∈RT ×2}K

3.3. Inference
Directly minimizing the energy defined in Eq. 1 is non-
trivial, as our energy function is highly non-linear and in-
volves millions of free variables. To address this, we de-
veloped a three-stage optimization pipeline, enabling us to
minimize the energy and estimate the scene variables in a
divide-and-conquer fashion.

Fusion.
From our energy minimization, we acquire a
semi-dense dynamic and static point cloud along with cam-
era parameters. To further densify the point cloud, enabling
each pixel to correspond to a 3D point, we perform depth-
based interpolation by computing a scale offset. Details can
be found in the supplementary.
To unify our outputs into a consistent 4D representation,
we use our camera parameters and static masks to project
the aligned depth maps into world coordinates. To handle
noisy depth values at boundaries, we create an edge mask
filter by thresholding gradients of the depth maps.

4. Experiments
Uni4D estimates camera pose, depth, and 3D motion from
a single video. We perform experiments evaluating its per-
formance with respect to baselines on these tasks.
4.1. Implementation Details
For optimization, we use the Adam optimizer with Re-
duceLROnPlateau and EarlyStopping in PyTorch [26, 42].
We perform 600 iterations per sliding window in stage 1,
2000 iterations in stage 2, and 1000 iterations in stage 3.
